title: Who was the first to 'spill the beans'? | SAYINGS EXPLAINED

entries.note: To reveal a secret, popularly traced to beans spilled from ancient Greek ballot hats, which the hosts doubt because the phrase first appears in 20th-century America.
The study of elections, from Greek [[from:psephos]], pebble, because the ancient Greeks voted by dropping pebbles into jars.
A modern phrase for revealing gossip, deliberate where [[see:spill the beans]] is accidental, from [[from:T]], late 20th-century Black drag slang for one's truth.
Black drag culture slang for one's truth, punningly written tea and used by [[see:The Lady Chablis]] in a 1994 interview; it gave [[gave:spill the tea]].
A major drag figure who appears in Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil and used [[see:T]] to mean her truth in a 1994 interview.
A meme about judging someone or listening in on a juicy conversation, which Jess suggests may have influenced [[see?:spill the tea]].
The French [[equivalent:spill the beans]], from accidentally leaving a mine's fuse sticking out so people can see where the bomb is.
The Spanish [[equivalent:spill the beans]]; the hosts aren't sure why a secret cake is involved.

entries.term: now the monkey comes out of the sleeve
entries.original: nu komt de aap uit de mouw
entries.translation: now the monkey comes out of the sleeve
entries.note: The Dutch [[equivalent:spill the beans]], possibly from a magic trick; the hosts say it has [[see:cat out of the bag]] energy.
Covered in an earlier idioms episode; unrelated to the [[unrelated:cat-o'-nine-tails]], it comes from buying a [[from:pig in a poke]] that turns out to be an unwanted cat.
A pig in a bag, bought unseen as a good animal but turning out to be a cat, the idea behind [[gave:cat out of the bag]].
Something one likes, recorded from 1908 and popularised by Punch in the 1930s, because everybody likes their tea a little differently.

entries.term: not for all the tea in China
entries.note: Meaning under no circumstances or at any price, from the late 19th century, because tea was a costly import.
A slightly newer version of [[from:tempest in a teapot]], with the same meaning.
Dates back to the early 1800s, slightly older than [[gave:storm in a teacup]].
Slang for coffee from the 1930s, best traced to [[from?:jamoke]]; theories involving [[see?:Josephus Daniels]] or the [[see?:average Joe]] are thought unlikely.
Late 19th-century American slang for coffee, a blend of [[from:java]] and [[from:mocha]], grouped with java and joe in 1930s naval glossaries.
US Secretary of the Navy who banned alcohol from officers' messes in 1914 by [[see:General Order 99]], an unsupported theory for [[see?:cup of Joe]].
The 1914 order by [[see:Josephus Daniels]] banning alcohol from officers' messes, which one unsupported theory links to [[see?:cup of Joe]].
The common man; one unlikely theory says [[see?:cup of Joe]] means the common fellow's cup.
Once a popular name for the everyman, like the Joe of [[see:average Joe]].
Once a popular name for the everyman, which is why we have [[gave:spotted dick]].
Named with [[from:Dick (name)]], once a popular name for the everyman.
Just a person's name, now applied to every person, like the everyman names [[see:Jack]] and [[see:Dick (name)]].
Originally 1800s stable slang for horses fed on beans before a race or hunt; it also once meant arrogant or purse-proud after sudden prosperity.

entries.original: parler français comme une vache espagnole
entries.note: Said of someone speaking a language badly, which the hosts find offensive to the Spanish and to cows.
In Old English the pupil, imagined as a small round fruit when [[see:apple]] meant any fruit; it translates the Hebrew [[from:little man of the eye]].
Once meant any kind of fruit, as discussed in an earlier episode, which is why the pupil became [[see:the apple of my eye]].
A Latin version of the same notion as [[equivalent:the apple of my eye]], used alongside it in Old English times.
Related to [[same-root:people]], because people looking into someone's eyes see a little reflection of themselves in the pupil.
A Hebrew phrase for the reflection of a person seen in someone's pupil, translated as [[gave:the apple of my eye]].
From Shakespeare's [[see:Antony and Cleopatra]], where Cleopatra calls them the days when she was [[see:green]] in judgment and cold in blood, meaning naive.
Taken from French, where it means lettuce, and earlier meaning something salted; in Germany it covers anything with lots of mayonnaise.
Means naive, like an unripe fruit, the sense Cleopatra puns on in [[see:salad days]].
Discussed in an earlier episode; brought up again while talking about sugary American fruit salads.
[[see:Cockney rhyming slang]] for stairs, the pairing Rob first thinks of for comparing apples.
A false comparison of similar-looking things, appearing in late 19th- and early 20th-century writing after replacing [[from:apples to oysters]]; now often used for very different things.
The 17th-century original, recorded by John Ray as 'as like as an apple to an oyster' for things with no resemblance; it gave [[gave:apples and oranges]].
The idea that one rotten apple spoils the rest, found in a 1528 Reformation pamphlet and earlier in a 1340 Kentish moral treatise.
Supposedly coined in 1976 by [[see:Tom Iacono]]; theories include a pun on [[from?:boob tuber]], looking potato-like when slouched, or being vegetative before the TV.
An American who supposedly coined [[see:couch potato]] in 1976 for himself and his TV-watching friends, but never explained the name.
A 1970s name for the television, still heard in the US, though to Rob it's a 1990s women's garment; it gave [[gave:boob tuber]].
Someone watching the [[from:boob tube]], punning on potatoes being tubers; one theory for [[gave?:couch potato]].

entries.term: how do you like them apples
entries.note: Found in 1895 in the Bryan Daily Eagle, boasting about cotton receipts and meaning how do you like those results; not from WWI [[unrelated:toffee apple]] shells.
A First World War name for a large spherical mortar shell, wrongly said to be behind [[unrelated:how do you like them apples]].
Literally means [[from:pomegranate]], which grenades resemble in shape and in scattering fragments like seeds.
Means grainy apple, its first part being French [[from:pomme]], apple; it gave [[gave:grenade]].
Mid-19th-century American slang for something desirable, applied to New York from the 1900s and made to stick by [[see:John J. Fitzgerald]] using it for New York's racetracks.
Late 19th- and early 20th-century term for a wager, showing the apple as a stand-in for something desirable, as in [[see:Big Apple]].
Morning Telegraph sportswriter who in 1921 used [[see:Big Apple]] for the New York racetracks, the country's richest circuit, making the name stick.
Often explained as putting a chip of wood on your shoulder and daring someone to knock it off, though Jess isn't sure that's true.
An American phrase recorded from 1891, so not from OED editor [[unrelated:C. T. Onions]]; possibly Cockney rhyming slang [[from?:onion rings]], supported by an early singular form.
Charles Talbut Onions, OED editor from 1922, wrongly said to be behind [[see:know your onions]], which is recorded before he went to university.
[[see:Cockney rhyming slang]] for things, one explanation of [[gave?:know your onions]], though Rob wonders why that phrase appeared first in America.
From [[from:Cockney rhyming slang]], and almost the only Cockney rhyming slang that has caught on in the United States.
Used constantly in Britain but, apart from [[see:blow a raspberry]], barely caught on in the US, which makes Rob doubt it explains [[see:know your onions]].
[[see:Cockney rhyming slang]] for the telephone, given as an example of how much the British use it.
Rob rejects the claim that it was a rack for cannonballs on ships, finding no such monkey in nautical guides or dialect books.
An adaptation of [[from:go ape]], from linking monkeys with bananas, though wild monkeys rarely eat them; it gave [[gave:bananas]].
Dates back to at least the early 1900s and was adapted into [[gave:go bananas]].
Became an idiom of its own, as in that's bananas, recorded from the 1920s and taken from [[from:go bananas]].
The sweet seedless banana we know, domesticated and not found in the wild, one reason wild monkeys rarely eat bananas despite [[see:go bananas]].
1920s slang for nonsense, from the nickname of artificial-smelling [[from:amyl acetate]], popularised by [[see:Rube Goldberg]]'s strips.
A 19th-century liquid smelling of bananas, used in paints, candy and perfume and nicknamed [[gave:banana oil]], known to be fake and overpowering.
Helped popularise [[see:banana oil]] in his strips as a word for nonsense, like baloney, applesauce or horsefeathers.
Jess links it with Old West scam artists selling an oil said to repel snakes, though she is unsure of the details.

entries.term: the proof of the pudding is in the eating
entries.note: Often misquoted as the proof is in the pudding; it uses [[see:prove]] in its old sense, to test, so the dish is tested by eating it.
Once meant to test, a sense surviving in [[see:proving ground]] and in [[see:the proof of the pudding is in the eating]].
A place where something is tested, keeping the old sense of [[from:prove]].
Means very different things: in the proverb, stuffed entrails like [[see:haggis]]; in Britain, sweet steamed dishes; in the US, something likely to contain bananas.
An example of the savoury kind of [[see:pudding]], as [[see:Robert Burns]] famously described it.
Primarily savoury in Britain but usually sweet in the US, like apple pie, or a pizza pie in New York.
A 19th-century phrase, more likely a pun on the lowly [[from:umble pie]] than coming directly from being served it.
A humble dish of [[from:umbles]] baked in a pie, whose sound made an irresistible pun giving [[gave:humble pie]].
Entrails, usually of a deer, a lowly food given to servants after aristocratic hunts, eaten long before the phrase [[see:humble pie]] existed.
Perfect order, first recorded in a British naval officer's 1780s diary; the reason is unknown, one theory being a mishearing of French [[from?:nappe pliée]], folded cloth.
Apple pie isn't especially American, but became a symbol through [[see:Johnny Appleseed]], early cookbooks, links with prosperity, and WWII soldiers fighting for [[see:mom and apple pie]].
A figure of the American frontier who linked apples with America, one route to [[see:American as apple pie]].
What WWII soldiers said they were fighting for, which may have cemented [[see:American as apple pie]].
Found from the 16th century, with equivalents in most European languages; probably from [[from?:Ecclesiastes]] 10:20, which warns that a bird may carry your voice.
Bitterness about something unattainable, from [[from:The Fox and the Grapes]]; an idiom from the 1760s, revived by [[see:Mark Twain]] in Tom Sawyer.
[[see:Aesop]]'s fable in which a fox fails to reach high grapes and declares them sour, the source of [[gave:sour grapes]].
Covered in one of the hosts' earlier idioms episodes.
Discussed in the hosts' first idioms episode, where its many theories wound viewers up.
